title: Broken Function-Level Authorization
subtopics: Preventing privileged actions through alternate routes
learning_outcomes: Explain how broken function-level authorization affects an API contract or implementation.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on broken function-level authorization in rest api security. You will connect protecting administrative endpoints to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Broken Function-Level Authorization matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying protecting administrative endpoints deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Authorization must be checked server-side for objects, functions, writable fields, tenants, and sensitive outputs. In this lesson, treat “Broken Function-Level Authorization” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Protecting administrative endpoints”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Role and permission checks” and “Authorization policy testing”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Assume every client-controlled value is untrusted and enforce security at the server boundary. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating broken function-level authorization. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.

content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Broken Function-Level Authorization with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating broken function-level authorization as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
